articles.summary: NASA’s Mars rover reaches major milestone with record-breaking journey  FOX WeatherThe Perseverance Rover Reaches Another Milestone  Universe TodayQuick space updates: Perseverance sets driving record, ice findings on Mars  WBAYmaxon Drives Support NASA’s Perseverance Rover on Mars Mission  Unmanned Systems TechnologyNASA's Perseverance Rover Breaks the Distance Record for Driving Off-World  Caltech
articles.full_text:
THE TAKEAWAY
- NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover broke a world record on Oct. 11.
- The rover drove the farthest distance on another world than any other vehicle.
- The milestone came when the rover was exploring traces of ancient hydrothermal systems.
NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover has set a world record for the farthest distance driven by any vehicle on the surface of another world.
On Oct. 11, the rover reached 28.10 miles, surpassing the previous record of 28.06 miles set by NASA’s Opportunity rover.
The milestone also marks three decades of NASA rover operations on Mars.
"The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving," Steven Lee, project manager for the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, said. "We’ve blown well past that, and with all mobility systems fully operational and favorable extended-ground-life test results, we expect Perseverance to keep adding to this record for many years to come."
The milestone came as Perseverance traveled toward an area called "Idubi," a region off the western rim of Jezero Crater, where the rover is investigating what may be some of the oldest terrain ever explored in the solar system.
According to NASA, the goal of the exploration is to find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems.
Using its autonomous navigation system, known as AutoNav, the rover captures images of the terrain while moving, builds a 3-D map of potential hazards and plots a course between waypoints selected by rover planners on Earth.
Perseverance has driven more than 90% of its total distance using AutoNav to evaluate the terrain, compared with about 5% for the first Martian AutoNav system on Opportunity.
"Our newest software teaches Perseverance to steer less and roll more, and to check its own position against orbital maps mid-drive," Mark Maimone, deputy team chief for robotic operations on Perseverance, said.
"The next frontier is sunlight itself. Glare in the navigation cameras is why we park by mid-afternoon if we’re driving toward the sun, and if we can teach the rover to see past those artifacts, every rover that follows gets a longer working day," he continued.

articles.title: Europe can’t lead on nature at COP17 while cutting biodiversity cash at home - EUobserver
articles.summary: Europe can’t lead on nature at COP17 while cutting biodiversity cash at home  EUobserver
articles.full_text:
For decades, the European Union has been a global leader in biodiversity protection. The Natura 2000 network, the Birds and Habitats Directives and, more recently, the Nature Restoration Regulation show that Europe has a strong legal framework.
At international level, the EU also played a decisive role in the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which was agreed in December 2022 at COP15 of the Convention on Biological Diversity. The framework established a global roadmap to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
Next week (19-30 October), Yerevan will host COP17 of the Convention, where the first global review of progress since the adoption of the Framework will take place. It will be an important opportunity to determine whether the commitments made are being translated into concrete action and results on the ground.
As co-chair of the European Parliament delegation attending the conference, I will defend a united European position that is consistent with our historic leadership and responds to the urgency of the challenge.
The European Commission, which formally negotiates on behalf of the Union on the basis of the position agreed with the member states, must promote decisions that accelerate implementation of the Global Biodiversity Framework during the remaining years to 2030.
Honest appraisal? A mixed picture
This global review must be accompanied by an honest assessment of our own performance. Europe should arrive in Yerevan acknowledging both the progress it has made and the work that remains.
The commission’s latest report on the implementation of the framework presents a mixed picture.
Of the 45 targets established for the EU, only two have been achieved and 16 are on track, while progress remains too slow on another 25 and two cannot yet be assessed.
There are positive signs in the EU. Protected areas have expanded, organic farming has increased and a greater proportion of fish stocks is being managed sustainably.
However, the overall situation of many habitats and species remains worrying, while farmland birds and grassland butterflies, among others, continue to decline.
The main problem is not a lack of legislation, as Europe already has many of the instruments it needs. The challenge is to implement them properly and turn them into visible improvements on the ground, which requires public authorities with sufficient capacity, reliable data, clear plans and stable funding.
The Nature Restoration Regulation is a good example.
Restoring wetlands, rivers, forests, soils and marine ecosystems will not only help biodiversity recover, but will also retain water, reduce flood damage, protect soils and make our territories more resilient to droughts, heatwaves and wildfires.
Missed deadlines
However, the regulation will only deliver results if member states meet their obligations.
The deadline for submitting draft national restoration plans was 1 September, yet only nine countries have done so.
This delay not only slows implementation, but also makes it harder to calculate the cost of restoring nature and the resources that will be required.
The commission was expected to present an assessment of restoration funding needs and gaps in August 2025, but we are still waiting for a complete analysis.
The commission argues that it needs the national plans to calculate these costs. Yet negotiations on the 2028-2034 financial framework are moving forward while many plans remain outstanding and we still lack a full estimate of the resources needed to implement one of our most important environmental laws.
This situation reflects one of the main challenges facing COP17.
Adopting targets is no longer enough. We must also agree on how they will be implemented, how progress will be measured and how action will be financed.
Five EU priorities in Yerevan
In this context, I believe that the European position should focus on five priorities. We must mobilise more resources for biodiversity, consolidate the Cali Fund, make progress in eliminating harmful subsidies, assess progress through concrete results and strengthen the role of nature in climate adaptation.
Finance will be one of the central issues in Yerevan, as the Global Biodiversity Framework calls for the mobilisation of at least $200bn [€178bn] a year from all sources by 2030. Public investment must remain the foundation of this effort, but private capital will also be needed.
With this aim, the commission presented its roadmap for nature credits in July 2025 and is now developing the methodologies, certification systems, oversight arrangements and pilot projects needed for their deployment.
These instruments could help finance conservation and restoration, but they will only be useful if they are governed by rigorous rules and deliver real, verifiable and additional benefits for biodiversity. They must never replace public funding or be used to justify damage to nature in one place in exchange for financing action elsewhere.
COP17 must also consolidate the Cali Fund, which was created so that companies benefiting from the use of digital information on genetic resources contribute to biodiversity conservation. The agreement reached at COP16 was an important step, but we now need real contributions and a fair distribution of resources, including for Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
Another priority must be to eliminate incentives and subsidies that harm biodiversity. It makes no sense to call for new resources to protect nature while public budgets continue to support activities that destroy it.
The European Union should therefore examine its own policies honestly, particularly in areas such as agriculture, fisheries, energy and infrastructure, and establish a timetable for progressively phasing out and ultimately eliminating this harmful support.
The global review must also measure concrete results. Success cannot be assessed simply by counting strategies or setting targets. We need to know whether ecosystems are recovering, whether species are in better condition, whether protected areas are being managed effectively and whether funding is actually reaching action on the ground.
We must also strengthen the connection between biodiversity and climate adaptation. The droughts, floods, heatwaves and wildfires affecting Europe show that protecting and restoring nature is not a secondary concern. Healthy ecosystems are among our best defences against the effects of climate change and represent a direct investment in our security, agriculture and economy.
All these priorities lead us inevitably to the European budget, because political commitments are only credible when they are backed by sufficient resources.
The budget?
There is currently a clear contradiction between the leadership that the European Union wishes to maintain on biodiversity and the place given to it in the proposal for the 2028-2034 financial framework.
Although the commission proposes that 35 percent of the next budget should contribute jointly to climate and environmental objectives, it removes the specific 10 percent target for biodiversity included in the current budget and no longer presents LIFE as a standalone programme.
By placing biodiversity within much broader objectives and funds, its financing becomes less visible and risks being pushed aside by priorities such as security, defence and competitiveness.
Parliament must defend sufficient and clearly identifiable resources for biodiversity and for the activities currently financed through LIFE.
Simplification can make funding easier to access, but it must not reduce environmental ambition, transparency or democratic oversight.
This budget debate also affects our international credibility. Europe cannot ask other countries to increase their ambition and financial contributions while weakening budgetary support for biodiversity within the Union itself. Our leadership in Yerevan will depend not only on what we defend in the negotiations, but also on what we are able to implement and finance at home.
Europe has strong laws, valuable experience and the capacity to lead. We do not need to start again. We need to deliver what we have already agreed, provide the necessary resources and use COP17 to accelerate global action.
The global review cannot be limited to describing how far we remain from the 2030 targets. It must help us agree on how to close that gap during the four years that remain. I will travel to Yerevan with the European Parliament delegation determined to support that objective.

articles.title: Cabka’s emission reduction targets validated by the Science Based Targets initiative - The Manila Times
articles.summary: Cabka’s emission reduction targets validated by the Science Based Targets initiative  The Manila Times
articles.full_text:
A major milestone in Cabka’s decarbonization journey
Amsterdam, Netherlands - 19 October 2026 - Cabka N.V. (together with its subsidiaries "Cabka”, or the "Company”), a company specialized in transforming hard to recycle plastic waste into innovative Reusable Transport Packaging (RTP), listed at Euronext Amsterdam, today announces that its near-term science-based emissions reduction targets have been validated by SBTi Services, the validation body of the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi). This important milestone provides a clear and measurable pathway for reducing emissions across our operations and value chain.
The validation builds on Cabka’s existing progress in reducing the carbon footprint of our operations and products, while continuing to expand the circular economy. Cabka committed to the set near-term science-based emissions reduction targets in 2024, aiming to achieve validation in 2026. This milestone has now been achieved on schedule.
"SBTi validation is an important milestone for Cabka,” said Alexander Masharov, CEO of Cabka. "Our priority is to deliver measurable emissions reductions through renewable electricity, more efficient operations and keeping more plastics in the loop. Expanding BuyBack and increasing the use of recycled materials will be central to turning our climate commitments into results.”
Validated targets
Cabka has set a target to reduce absolute scope 1 and 2 GHG emissions by 79.79% by 2030 from a 2022 base year. We have also set a target to reduce absolute scope 3 GHG emissions from purchased goods and services and the end-of-life treatment of sold products by 35.0% by 2036 from a 2022 base year.
Measurable progress
From 2022 to 2025, Cabka’s market-based scope 1 and 2 emissions decreased by approximately 66%, driven by the switch to renewable electricity across our sites. That is more than four fifths of the distance to the validated 2030 target. Over the same period, total reported scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, including exclusions, fell by approximately 15%.
Scope 3 remains the largest share of Cabka’s footprint. Reducing it, through raw material choices and the end-of-life treatment of sold products, is the focus of the 2036 target.
Ambition beyond the validated targets
The validated targets define our science-based pathway. On this basis, we continue to pursue our broader company ambition of 100% renewable energy and carbon-neutral own operations by 2030. That ambition goes beyond the validated targets and continues to guide our investment choices.
We will keep reducing emissions across our operations and value chain, with circularity, renewable electricity, energy efficiency and material choices at the heart of our approach.
For more information about Cabka and its sustainability activities, visit Cabka.com.

About Cabka
Cabka is in the business of recycling plastics from post-consumer and post-industrial waste into innovative reusable transport packaging (RTP), such as pallets and large container solutions, helping to improve sustainability across the logistics chain. ECO products are mainly construction and road safety products produced exclusively out of post-consumer waste.
Cabka is leading the industry in its integrated approach, closing the loop from waste to recycling to manufacturing. Backed by its own innovation center, it has the rare industry knowledge, capability, and capacity to maximize the use of recycled plastics by bringing them back into the production loop. Cabka is fully equipped to capture value across the full chain from waste to end products.
Cabka is listed at Euronext Amsterdam as of 1 March 2022 under the CABKA ticker with international securities identification number NL00150000S7.

articles.title: ESMA Sets 2026 Enforcement Priorities for Financial, ESG Reporting
articles.summary:
The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) has established its 2026 enforcement priorities, placing financial uncertainty and sustainability reporting quality at the centre of regulatory scrutiny. The priorities will guide […]
The post ESMA Sets 2026 Enforcement Priorities for Financial, ESG Reporting appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
ESMA Sets 2026 Enforcement Priorities for Financial, ESG Reporting
- ESG reporting scrutiny: ESMA will prioritise materiality assessments and connections between sustainability risks, corporate policies, targets, and reported metrics.
- Financial disclosure risks: Geopolitical uncertainty, restructuring provisions, and debt restructuring will face increased regulatory attention in 2026 annual reports.
- Investor protection: European regulators will target reporting inconsistencies and digital filing errors while pursuing simpler disclosure requirements.
The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) has established its 2026 enforcement priorities, placing financial uncertainty and sustainability reporting quality at the centre of regulatory scrutiny.
The priorities will guide national regulators when reviewing annual financial reports from listed companies across the European Union.
ESMA’s European Common Enforcement Priorities (ECEP) cover International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), and digital reporting requirements.
The regulator is seeking more consistent disclosures as companies navigate geopolitical disruption, financial restructuring, and evolving sustainability obligations.
For corporate boards and investors, the priorities clarify where European supervisors expect stronger evidence, transparency, and accountability.
Sustainability Reporting Faces Closer Examination
Sustainability disclosures remain a central enforcement focus as companies continue implementing the European Sustainability Reporting Standards.
ESMA has identified two areas requiring particular attention: materiality assessments and the consistency of information presented across sustainability statements.
Under ESRS, companies must assess both their impacts on people and the environment and the financial relevance of sustainability matters.
These assessments determine which environmental, social, and governance issues require disclosure.
ESMA expects companies to demonstrate continued progress in applying materiality assessments rather than treating them as procedural exercises.
The regulator will also examine how companies connect their identified impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) with policies, actions, and targets (PATs).
Reported sustainability metrics must provide a coherent account of corporate performance and strategic commitments.
This approach places greater responsibility on management teams to demonstrate how sustainability risks influence operational decisions and corporate governance.
For investors, stronger connections between disclosures could improve assessments of transition risks, corporate resilience, and long-term financial exposure.
Geopolitical Risks and Corporate Restructuring Under Review
ESMA’s financial reporting priorities reflect growing uncertainty across international markets.
Geopolitical risks and their implications for IFRS financial statements will receive particular attention.
Companies must consider how external disruptions affect financial assumptions, asset valuations, liabilities, and other material reporting judgments.
The regulator has also prioritised restructuring provisions and debt restructuring.
These areas can involve significant management judgment, particularly when companies face operational pressures or changes in financing arrangements.
For auditors and supervisory bodies, the priorities establish a common framework for examining whether financial statements appropriately reflect material uncertainties.
The emphasis also reinforces the importance of consistency between financial reporting and sustainability disclosures.
Where climate-related or geopolitical risks affect business operations, investors need to understand their potential financial consequences.
RELATED ARTICLE: ESMA, EU Environment Agency Tighten Ties on Sustainable Finance Oversight
Digital Reporting Errors Remain an Enforcement Concern
ESMA will also scrutinise compliance with the European Single Electronic Format (ESEF), which supports standardised digital financial reporting.
The regulator has identified recurring filing errors involving statements of changes in equity.
These errors can affect the accuracy and usability of electronically reported financial information.
Addressing them forms part of ESMA’s broader effort to improve the reliability and comparability of corporate disclosures.
Separately, ESMA published its 31st extract from the Financial Reporting Working Group’s enforcement database.
The publication contains seven decisions concerning IFRS Accounting Standards and ESMA’s Guidelines on Alternative Performance Measures.
These decisions provide additional insight into how European supervisors assess reporting practices and apply existing requirements.
Regulatory Simplification Meets Investor Protection
ESMA’s enforcement agenda comes amid broader European efforts to reduce corporate reporting complexity.
The authority reaffirmed its commitment to simplification and burden reduction while maintaining investor protection and financial market stability.
Materiality remains central to that balance.
Companies should focus disclosures on information relevant to investors and other stakeholders without compromising reporting quality.
ESMA expects issuers, auditors, and supervisory bodies to consider its recommendations when preparing and reviewing annual reports.
Their application should reflect each company’s operations, materiality assessments, and reporting circumstances.
For multinational businesses operating in European capital markets, the priorities provide an early indication of supervisory expectations.
They also reinforce the growing importance of aligning sustainability disclosures with financial reporting and corporate risk management.
As European reporting requirements evolve, enforcement consistency will remain critical to investor confidence and the credibility of sustainability information across global capital markets.

articles.title: CarbonFarm Raises $8.2 Million to Scale Rice Methane Reduction Technology
articles.summary:
CarbonFarm Secures Funding to Expand Agricultural Decarbonisation French climate technology company CarbonFarm has raised approximately $8.2 million in an oversubscribed Series A round to accelerate methane reduction across global rice […]
The post CarbonFarm Raises $8.2 Million to Scale Rice Methane Reduction Technology appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
CarbonFarm Raises $8.2 Million to Scale Rice Methane Reduction Technology
- $8.2 million Series A funding: CarbonFarm secures investment led by Colam Impact, with participation from Suma Capital, Proparco and other investors.
- Global agricultural decarbonisation: The company operates across 19 countries, using satellite technology to measure methane reductions and support climate finance.
- Rice methane reduction potential: Improved water management can reduce methane emissions by up to 50%, according to the International Rice Research Institute.
CarbonFarm Secures Funding to Expand Agricultural Decarbonisation
French climate technology company CarbonFarm has raised approximately $8.2 million in an oversubscribed Series A round to accelerate methane reduction across global rice production.
Colam Impact led the financing, with Suma Capital participating through its SC Climate Tech Ventures I fund. Other investors included Proparco, elea, Working Capital Fund, Albo and BPI France. Existing investors Serena and Techmind also participated.
The investment will support CarbonFarm’s expansion across Asia, Africa and Europe while accelerating its entry into Latin America. Funding will also strengthen its satellite monitoring technology and agricultural project development capabilities.
For Suma Capital, the transaction is its first investment outside Spain through SC Climate Tech Ventures I. The firm identified CarbonFarm’s proprietary technology, project execution capabilities and recurring commercial relationships as key investment factors.
Satellite Monitoring Connects Methane Reductions With Climate Finance
Rice cultivation is essential to global food security but remains a significant source of agricultural methane emissions. Flooded rice paddies create oxygen-depleted conditions that encourage methane production.
CarbonFarm addresses this challenge through digital Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) technology.
Its platform combines satellite imagery, ground-level agricultural data and greenhouse gas calculation models. This enables emissions monitoring at individual plot level and verification of changes in farming practices.
One approach involves alternating periods of flooding and drying in rice paddies. According to the International Rice Research Institute, this technique can reduce methane emissions by up to 50%.
Reliable verification is central to attracting climate finance. Agricultural projects must demonstrate measurable emissions reductions to support carbon credit issuance and corporate decarbonisation claims.
Xavier Sánchez, Partner at Suma Capital, said: “CarbonFarm tackles one of the main challenges of agricultural decarbonisation: turning changes in farming practices into impact that is measurable, verifiable and financeable. Its combination of proprietary technology, knowledge of rice cultivation and on-the-ground execution capability fits squarely with our thesis of investing in scalable climate solutions for hard-to-abate sectors. At Suma Capital, we want to support the company in this new stage, contributing our experience in growth, strategic planning and partnership development within the agri-food sector.”
Projects Across 19 Countries Target Agricultural Emissions
CarbonFarm has operated in 19 countries, collaborating with farmers, cooperatives, agricultural companies, development organisations and public authorities.
In Vietnam, the company participates in the TRVC project alongside international development organisation SNV. The initiative aims to establish 200,000 hectares of low-emission rice cultivation by 2028.
In Spain, CarbonFarm supports Ebro Group’s Oryzonte project, which encourages water-efficient rice cultivation in Seville. Similar collaborations extend to Ebro’s Tilda brand in the UK and its operations in India.
RELATED ARTICLE: EU Sets Global Standard for Methane Emissions Reductions
Its wider network includes Mars Food, Diageo, Livelihoods Funds, myclimate, the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.
These partnerships connect agricultural emissions reductions with corporate supply chains, development finance and voluntary carbon markets.
Local Partnerships Drive Scalable Climate Investment
CarbonFarm’s expansion strategy relies on equipping established agricultural networks rather than replacing existing relationships with farming communities.
Vassily Carantino, co-founder and CEO of CarbonFarm, said: “Scale will not come from replacing local players in the value chain, but from equipping them with the tools they need. They know the farming systems and have the relationships needed to drive change. Our role is to help turn that local knowledge into programmes capable of attracting funding and delivering results that can withstand rigorous scrutiny.”
Suma Capital will support commercial introductions, access to public funding and strategic development.
For food manufacturers and investors, the technology offers a mechanism to connect agricultural practices with measurable climate outcomes.
Verified emissions data can strengthen Scope 3 reporting, inform supply chain investment and support financing decisions. However, credible methodologies and independent verification remain essential to maintaining confidence in reported reductions.
As agricultural methane attracts greater attention in global climate policy, CarbonFarm’s expansion highlights growing investment in technologies that connect emissions measurement with practical farming interventions.
For rice-producing economies, the opportunity extends beyond carbon markets. More efficient water management and access to climate finance could help farmers reduce emissions while strengthening the resilience of global food supply chains.

articles.title: Sosteneo Clean Energy Fund II Secures $525 Million for European Infrastructure
articles.summary:
Sosteneo, part of Generali Investments, has secured more than $175 million in new commitments and co-investment capital at the first external close of its second clean energy infrastructure fund. The […]
The post Sosteneo Clean Energy Fund II Secures $525 Million for European Infrastructure appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Sosteneo Clean Energy Fund II Secures $525 Million for European Infrastructure
- Capital commitments: Sosteneo Fund II secures over $175 million in new commitments and co-investment capital, bringing its vintage total above $525 million.
- Institutional backing: Generali Insurance Companies increases its commitment alongside returning and new institutional investors, expanding Sosteneo’s investor base.
- Energy transition investment: Fund II targets construction-ready European infrastructure supporting renewable energy integration, clean power supply, and industrial decarbonisation.
Sosteneo, part of Generali Investments, has secured more than $175 million in new commitments and co-investment capital at the first external close of its second clean energy infrastructure fund.
The fundraising brings total commitments for the Fund II vintage above $525 million. Sosteneo’s wider investment platform now manages more than $1.28 billion in committed capital.
The close strengthens the firm’s position in Europe’s clean energy infrastructure market, where investment demand continues to grow alongside electricity system modernisation and industrial decarbonisation requirements.
Institutional Investors Expand Support for Clean Energy Infrastructure
The first external close combines renewed commitments from existing investors with capital from new institutional partners.
The largest external institutional investor in Sosteneo Clean Energy Infrastructure Fund I has committed additional capital to Fund II. Generali Insurance Companies, the cornerstone investor in Sosteneo’s flagship funds, has also increased its commitment.
Together, these investments broaden the fund’s institutional investor base and provide additional capacity for European infrastructure deployment.
Chris Deves, Partner and Head of Investor Relations at Sosteneo, commented: “This is an important milestone for Fund II. We are pleased to have the renewed support of an existing institutional investor, alongside commitments from new investors. We see this as a strong endorsement of our strategy and the progress we have made to date. The close also further broadens our institutional investor base and provides a strong foundation as we continue the Fund II raise.”
The commitments come as infrastructure investors increasingly assess how clean energy assets can deliver predictable returns while supporting long-term decarbonisation objectives.
Fund I Begins Distributions as Operational Assets Mature
Sosteneo’s fundraising progress follows the continued development of its first clean energy infrastructure portfolio.
Approximately three-quarters of Fund I’s 39 projects are now fully operational, three years after the fund’s inception.
During the second quarter, Fund I began distributing income generated by operating portfolio assets to investors.
In the third quarter, the fund also signed an agreement to sell an interest in an operating asset, representing its first partial realisation.
These developments demonstrate the portfolio’s transition from construction and development towards income generation and capital recycling.
Umberto Tamburrino, Managing Partner and CEO at Sosteneo, commented: “We are pleased with the continued progress of Fund I, with most projects now fully operational after just three years from inception. The commencement of income distributions and the signing of our first partial realisation represent further steps in the maturation of the portfolio. Fund I continues to progress in line with our expectations, providing a strong foundation as we continue to develop the Sosteneo platform and deploy Fund II.”
RELATED ARTICLE: Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners Buys Ørsted’s European Onshore Renewables For $1.7 Billion
Fund II Targets Europe’s Energy Transition Infrastructure
Fund II will focus on construction-ready clean energy infrastructure across European markets.
Its strategy prioritises physical assets capable of generating stable, visible, long-term cash flows.
Investment opportunities span three areas: infrastructure enabling energy system integration and flexibility, assets securing clean energy supply, and projects supporting industrial decarbonisation.
Sosteneo aims to create value through specialist capabilities in construction management, project financing, and revenue contracting.
These capabilities are particularly relevant as European electricity systems integrate greater volumes of renewable generation while managing grid constraints and changing demand patterns.
Investment Strategy Aligns Financial Returns With Decarbonisation
For institutional investors, Sosteneo’s fundraising illustrates the growing role of private infrastructure capital in financing Europe’s energy transition.
The strategy combines exposure to physical clean energy assets with an emphasis on contracted revenues and operational resilience.
However, construction execution, financing conditions, and electricity market developments remain important considerations for investors evaluating infrastructure returns.
The progression of Fund I provides an operating track record as Sosteneo seeks additional commitments for Fund II.
With more than $1.28 billion in platform commitments, Sosteneo is positioned to expand investment across European energy infrastructure.
Its next phase will test how effectively institutional capital can translate construction-ready projects into operational assets that support Europe’s energy security, industrial competitiveness, and long-term climate objectives.

articles.title: Mirova’s $1 Billion Natural Capital Strategy Targets Climate Resilience
articles.summary:
Mirova Positions Nature as Critical Economic Infrastructure Sustainable investment manager Mirova is expanding its natural capital investment approach, positioning ecosystem restoration as essential infrastructure for economic resilience and climate security. […]
The post Mirova’s $1 Billion Natural Capital Strategy Targets Climate Resilience appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Mirova’s $1 Billion Natural Capital Strategy Targets Climate Resilience
- $1 billion raised: Mirova’s natural capital platform has supported more than 70 projects across carbon solutions, regenerative agriculture and ecosystem restoration.
- Measurable environmental impact: Its carbon solutions portfolio reports 4.9 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent sequestered or avoided and 1.1 million hectares restored or conserved.
- Strategic investment expansion: Mirova is exploring a European bioeconomy strategy to reduce fossil resource dependence and strengthen regional supply chains.
Mirova Positions Nature as Critical Economic Infrastructure
Sustainable investment manager Mirova is expanding its natural capital investment approach, positioning ecosystem restoration as essential infrastructure for economic resilience and climate security.
Its 2025 Natural Capital Impact Report details more than $1 billion raised since inception and over 70 projects supported globally.
The strategy reflects growing financial exposure to biodiversity loss, soil degradation and declining ecosystem productivity.
More than half of global GDP, approximately $58 trillion, is moderately or highly dependent on nature, according to research cited in the report.
Mirova argues that protecting these resources requires the same long-term investment discipline applied to conventional infrastructure.
Gautier Quéru, Global Head of Natural Capital at Mirova, stated:
“Nature is not a backdrop to the economy. It is its foundation. Our responsibility now is to preserve and regenerate it as strategic infrastructure, supporting climate resilience, our sovereignty and long-term prosperity.”
Investment Platform Expands Across Carbon and Agriculture
Established in 2015, Mirova’s dedicated natural capital platform combines investment expertise with carbon finance, agronomy and ESG management.
Its investment activities concentrate on carbon solutions and regenerative food systems, alongside plans to explore European bioeconomy opportunities.
Carbon investments support reforestation, ecosystem conservation, agroforestry and improved land management.
The report identifies 4.9 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent in current sequestered or avoided emissions across its carbon solutions portfolio.
Projects also report approximately 1.1 million hectares restored or conserved, alongside 141,101 beneficiaries and 11,262 jobs created or supported.
However, reported emissions impacts currently cover only two conservation projects. Several other investments remain in early development.
The distinction matters for institutional investors assessing projected environmental benefits against verified outcomes.
Carbon Integrity and ESG Governance Shape Investment Decisions
Mirova applies environmental and social safeguards throughout the investment lifecycle, from initial screening to post-investment monitoring.
Projects undergo ESG due diligence, with contractual Environmental and Social Action Plans addressing identified risks.
Quarterly monitoring and annual performance reviews provide oversight of implementation.
Its carbon integrity framework examines measurability, additionality, permanence, social benefits and biodiversity outcomes.
The platform also evaluates carbon credit buyers, requiring credible decarbonisation commitments rather than reliance on offsets as their primary climate strategy.
RELATED ARTICLE: Mirova Launches €2 Billion Energy Transition Infrastructure Fund
These controls address growing investor scrutiny of voluntary carbon markets, particularly concerning credit quality and environmental claims.
In Peru, the Nii Kaniti project illustrates this approach.
Developed with seven Indigenous communities, the initiative protects approximately 114,863 hectares of Amazon rainforest.
During 2025, 256 community members participated in forest patrols, supporting conservation and local livelihoods.
European Bioeconomy Strategy Targets Supply Chain Resilience
Mirova is also exploring a third investment strategy focused on Europe’s bioeconomy.
The proposed approach would finance companies, production assets and projects using renewable biological resources across agriculture, forestry and energy.
Its objective is to support alternatives to fossil-based materials while strengthening regional industrial resilience.
Geopolitical tensions and supply chain vulnerabilities have increased the strategic importance of domestic biological resources.
For European policymakers, the bioeconomy offers potential benefits across food security, industrial competitiveness and climate adaptation.
However, scaling biological alternatives requires sustainable resource management to avoid transferring environmental pressures onto land and ecosystems.
Natural Capital Moves Into Strategic Investment Planning
For executives and institutional investors, Mirova’s approach places ecosystem degradation within broader financial risk management.
Agricultural productivity, raw material security and carbon market credibility increasingly depend on functioning natural systems.
The investment challenge extends beyond financing restoration. Projects must demonstrate durable environmental outcomes, credible governance and commercially sustainable operations.
Mirova’s expansion reflects a wider opportunity to integrate natural capital into infrastructure investment and industrial strategy.
As governments pursue climate resilience and greater economic autonomy, financing healthy ecosystems could become increasingly important to long-term competitiveness across developed and emerging markets.

articles.summary:
Anthropic is establishing a new equity-backed public benefit fund designed to direct a growing share of its corporate value toward societal priorities. The initiative connects the artificial intelligence developer’s financial […]

articles.full_text:
Anthropic Commits 5% Equity to Public Benefit Fund as AI Valuation Grows
- Equity commitment: Anthropic plans to allocate 5% of its shares to a new Public Benefit Fund, subject to stockholder approval, with potential increases tied to company valuation.
- Economic and social impact: The initiative builds on Anthropic’s $200 million commitment to address AI-driven labor market disruption and support broader public benefit initiatives.
- Corporate governance: Approximately 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to public benefit commitments when existing founder and employee pledges are included, with further allocations possible.
Anthropic is establishing a new equity-backed public benefit fund designed to direct a growing share of its corporate value toward societal priorities. The initiative connects the artificial intelligence developer’s financial growth with commitments to address the technology’s economic and social consequences.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will initially receive 5% of company shares, subject to stockholder approval. Its structure also allows the board to allocate an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s valuation above a predetermined baseline.
The arrangement creates a mechanism through which rising corporate valuations could translate into additional resources for public benefit initiatives.
Linking Corporate Growth to Public Benefit
Anthropic operates as a public benefit corporation, a legal structure requiring consideration of public benefits alongside financial interests.
Much of its existing mission-related work remains within the business. This includes AI safety research, interpretability studies, biomedical research, and discounted access to Claude for nonprofit organizations and scientific institutions.
These activities combine commercial value with broader societal objectives.
The new fund will provide greater flexibility to support initiatives beyond Anthropic’s core operations. Potential activities include substantial donations to established nonprofits and direct financial distributions to specific populations.
Anthropic explained its approach: “Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good.” The company also contrasted the arrangement with conventional executive compensation structures. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.”
Addressing AI’s Economic Disruption
Labor market disruption is among the fund’s potential priorities.
AI adoption could generate substantial economic gains while exposing workers and industries to employment instability. The distribution of those gains is becoming an increasingly important consideration for policymakers, employers, and investors.
Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing labor market impacts.
However, the company acknowledged that accelerating technological development could require more ambitious interventions.
The fund could provide an additional financing mechanism for initiatives addressing workforce displacement, economic adjustment, and other consequences of AI deployment.
For corporate leaders, these concerns extend beyond workforce planning. They also raise questions about responsible automation, social stability, and the allocation of productivity gains.
Governance Structure and Political Restrictions
Anthropic will establish the fund as a wholly owned limited liability company rather than a traditional nonprofit organization.
The structure is intended to provide flexibility across different forms of charitable giving and direct financial support.
Importantly, Anthropic states that equity held by the fund will not finance lobbying or political contributions, either domestically or internationally.
RELATED ARTICLE: Anthropic CEO Rejects Open-Weights Ban, Calls for AI Chip Controls and Safety Testing
The restriction establishes a boundary between the fund’s public benefit activities and political influence.
However, several governance details remain outstanding. Anthropic plans to disclose further information about the fund’s oversight arrangements and valuation thresholds in the coming months.
These disclosures will be important for evaluating accountability, decision-making authority, and the mechanisms governing future equity allocations.
Founder Commitments Expand Public Benefit Allocation
The initiative builds on earlier commitments from Anthropic’s founders and employees.
At the company’s founding, its co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their personal equity holdings.
Anthropic also operates an employee equity donation matching programme, with approximately half its workforce participating.
Combined with the new fund, these arrangements mean roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to public benefit commitments, according to the company.
Additional allocations could follow if specified valuation thresholds are reached.
Anthropic intends to publish a public benefit report detailing progress against its corporate mission.
For investors and corporate boards, the arrangement introduces a notable approach to linking equity ownership with social responsibility.
Its effectiveness will depend on governance transparency, the deployment of resources, and measurable outcomes.
As AI companies accumulate economic influence, Anthropic’s model adds to the debate over how technology-generated wealth should support public interests and mitigate the risks associated with rapid automation.

articles.title: Banks Lend $595 Billion to Companies Linked to Tropical Deforestation
articles.summary:
Banks have provided nearly $600 billion in financing to companies associated with tropical deforestation and ecosystem destruction since 2020, according to new research. The findings expose growing financial exposure to […]
The post Banks Lend $595 Billion to Companies Linked to Tropical Deforestation appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Banks Lend $595 Billion to Companies Linked to Tropical Deforestation
- $595 billion in financing: Banks provided $351 billion to high-risk agricultural commodity companies and $244 billion to mining firms between 2020 and 2025.
- Forest-risk lending accelerates: Annual agricultural commodity financing increased 71% since 2016, while mining finance rose 55%, driven partly by lithium and nickel demand.
- Biodiversity safeguards fall short: Environmental groups warn that major lenders lack adequate protections as governments face mounting pressure to meet global conservation targets.
Banks have provided nearly $600 billion in financing to companies associated with tropical deforestation and ecosystem destruction since 2020, according to new research.
The findings expose growing financial exposure to industries linked to forest loss, land degradation and biodiversity decline. They also raise questions about banks’ environmental risk management as governments prepare to assess progress toward global conservation commitments.
The Forests & Finance coalition published the findings in its annual Banking on Biodiversity Collapse report.
Between 2020 and 2025, banks extended $351 billion in credit to high-risk agricultural commodity companies and another $244 billion to mining firms.
“These sectors are the primary drivers of deforestation, land degradation and community conflict across the tropical forest basins of South America, Southeast Asia and Central and West Africa,” the coalition said.
Forest-Risk Financing Continues to Accelerate
Despite expanding corporate sustainability commitments, financing for industries associated with tropical forest destruction has increased substantially over the past decade.
Annual lending and underwriting to mining companies operating in tropical forest-rich countries rose 55% between 2016 and 2025.
Financing increased from $23.7 billion to $36.7 billion, with lithium and nickel accounting for some of the largest increases.
Both minerals are critical inputs for electric vehicles, batteries and clean energy infrastructure.
Their growing financing needs create a challenge for financial institutions seeking to support decarbonisation while protecting biodiversity.
Mining projects can introduce environmental risks through land clearing, habitat fragmentation and pressure on local communities.
Agricultural commodity financing has expanded even faster.
Annual forest-risk financing increased 71% since 2016, climbing from $37.9 billion to $64.7 billion.
Within that increase, financing for beef production rose more than 50%. Soy financing expanded 137%, while lending to pulp and paper companies increased 157%.
These industries remain major sources of pressure on tropical forests, particularly where agricultural expansion intersects with weak land-use enforcement.
Indonesia Faces Growing Environmental and Financial Risks
Indonesia illustrates the consequences of continued financing for forest-intensive industries.
According to the coalition, banks provided $67.1 billion to Indonesia’s pulp and palm oil sectors between 2020 and 2025.
The report links these activities to deforestation and peatland drainage, particularly across Kalimantan and Sumatra.
Peatlands store substantial quantities of carbon. Draining them increases emissions and makes surrounding landscapes more vulnerable to fires.
Forest degradation can also worsen flooding by reducing the landscape’s ability to absorb rainfall.
Indonesia is experiencing its most intense El Niño-fuelled wildfire season in 11 years.
Smoke from the fires has contributed to deteriorating air quality across Southeast Asia, including Singapore and Malaysia.
The resulting haze has increased respiratory illnesses and exposed the regional consequences of forest degradation.
For banks, these developments create potential exposure to physical climate risks, regulatory intervention and reputational damage.
RELATED ARTICLE: EU Deforestation Law Could Reshape Global Coffee Trade
Banks Face Scrutiny Over Biodiversity Safeguards
The coalition argues that existing environmental policies have failed to keep pace with financing activity.
Banks “issuing the most high-risk credit still do not have adequate safeguards to mitigate the risks of serious environmental and social harm,” it said.
The findings raise questions about how lenders assess biodiversity impacts across corporate lending portfolios.
For financial institutions, stronger due diligence could include reviewing deforestation exposure, land-use practices and environmental compliance before extending credit.
Investors also face growing pressure to examine whether sustainability commitments translate into effective financing restrictions.
The distinction matters as biodiversity loss increasingly enters financial risk assessments alongside climate-related exposures.
Global Biodiversity Talks Increase Pressure on Finance
The report arrives as governments gather in Yerevan, Armenia, on October 19 for another round of international biodiversity negotiations.
A planned assessment of progress toward 2030 conservation targets is expected to reveal substantial implementation gaps.
The discussions take place against the backdrop of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which calls for greater alignment between financial flows and biodiversity protection.
For banks and institutional investors, the central challenge is increasingly financial as well as environmental.
Continued lending to forest-risk industries could expose portfolios to tightening regulation, supply chain disruption and rising ecosystem-related losses.
The findings also highlight a broader contradiction in sustainable finance: capital supporting economic development and the energy transition can simultaneously accelerate nature loss.
How financial institutions address that tension will influence biodiversity outcomes across tropical forest regions and the credibility of global conservation commitments.

articles.summary:
LanzaJet Secures New Capital to Expand SAF Production LanzaJet has secured at least $20 million in committed financing to accelerate sustainable aviation fuel production at its Freedom Pines Fuels facility […]
The post LanzaJet Secures $20 Million to Scale Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
LanzaJet Secures $20 Million to Scale Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production
- $20 million in new financing will support LanzaJet’s commercial expansion and production ramp-up at its Freedom Pines Fuels facility in Georgia.
- 10 million gallons of annual production capacity positions Freedom Pines Fuels to supply sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) to global customers.
- LanzaTech will increase its ownership stake as part of a broader recapitalization, strengthening financial oversight and supporting LanzaJet’s commercial growth.
LanzaJet Secures New Capital to Expand SAF Production
LanzaJet has secured at least $20 million in committed financing to accelerate sustainable aviation fuel production at its Freedom Pines Fuels facility in Soperton, Georgia.
The financing supports the company’s next phase of commercial operations as aviation faces mounting pressure to reduce emissions and secure reliable supplies of lower-carbon fuels.
The first financing close occurred on October 14, with the full transaction expected to conclude by December 2026.
LanzaTech Global, investor Vinod Khosla and LanzaJet’s Board are supporting the financing. The investment forms part of a broader recapitalization and debt reduction initiative backed by existing shareholders and investors.
Under the restructuring, LanzaTech will significantly increase its ownership of LanzaJet, strengthening its influence over the company’s commercial strategy.
The financing comes as SAF producers face the challenge of converting technological progress into commercially viable, large-scale production.
Freedom Pines Fuels Targets Commercial Scale
Freedom Pines Fuels is the world’s first commercial-scale alcohol-to-jet production facility, with annual production capacity of 10 million gallons.
The Georgia facility has already produced SAF and renewable diesel that meet ASTM specifications, demonstrating the technology’s ability to manufacture fuels that satisfy established industry standards.
The new financing will support production increases and enable LanzaJet to expand deliveries to international customers.
However, achieving sustained commercial output remains critical. SAF developers must balance production costs, feedstock availability and customer demand while competing against conventional jet fuel.
LanzaJet’s alcohol-to-jet technology converts ethanol into aviation fuel, offering an alternative production pathway to conventional SAF processes.
Its technology can process ethanol derived from multiple sources, reducing dependence on individual feedstocks or geographic markets.
Established ethanol industries in Brazil and the United States provide potential supply opportunities. Regional agricultural resources and waste-derived ethanol offer additional pathways for localized production.
LanzaTech’s gas fermentation platform can also convert waste-carbon resources into ethanol, potentially expanding the range of eligible feedstocks.
This flexibility is particularly relevant in markets with sustainability requirements governing SAF eligibility.
Regulatory Requirements Shape Global SAF Markets
SAF production is becoming increasingly important as governments introduce policies to reduce aviation emissions.
The European Union’s ReFuelEU Aviation framework requires aviation fuel suppliers to progressively increase the proportion of SAF supplied at designated EU airports.
The United Kingdom has also introduced SAF requirements, creating demand for qualifying lower-carbon aviation fuels.
These policies place greater emphasis on feedstock sustainability, lifecycle emissions and regulatory compliance.
LanzaJet’s ability to source ethanol from different production pathways could help projects adapt to regional requirements while managing feedstock costs.
For airlines and fuel suppliers, access to compliant SAF remains a commercial priority. Production capacity alone does not guarantee supply, particularly when eligible feedstocks face competing demand.
RELATED ARTICLE: Airbus and LanzaJet to Collaborate on Sustainable Aviation Fuel Production
LanzaTech Strengthens Ownership and Leadership Oversight
The recapitalization also introduces greater leadership continuity as LanzaJet moves toward expanded commercial operations.
Jennifer Holmgren, Chief Executive Officer of LanzaTech, will remain Chair of LanzaJet’s Board while serving as interim CEO.
The Board considers experienced leadership and operational continuity essential during the company’s next development phase.
“LanzaJet has exceptional people, differentiated technology and an important role to play in scaling sustainable aviation fuel,” said Jennifer Holmgren, Chief Executive Officer of LanzaTech and Chair and interim CEO of LanzaJet.
“LanzaTech began developing alcohol-to-jet technology in 2012 in partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, and since 2020, LanzaJet has had the strong backing of global investors and funders. LanzaTech has taken first-of-a-kind technology to profitable commercial operation. With a larger ownership stake and the Board’s full support, we look forward to bringing Freedom Pines Fuels and future LanzaJet plants to the same commercial success.”
Commercial Execution Becomes the Next Test for SAF Investment
For investors, LanzaJet’s financing illustrates the capital requirements facing emerging clean-fuel technologies as they transition from demonstration to commercial operations.
The restructuring provides additional financial support while concentrating ownership and governance responsibility.
For aviation executives, the immediate priority is whether Freedom Pines Fuels can translate its production capacity into dependable SAF deliveries.
Longer term, the company’s ethanol flexibility could support projects across multiple markets, particularly where regulatory mandates encourage investment in qualifying low-carbon fuels.
As aviation decarbonization requirements expand, LanzaJet’s next phase will test whether alcohol-to-jet technology can achieve the commercial performance needed to support global SAF supply.
